title: Pneumoperitoneum & Steep Trendelenburg Physiology
keywords: raised intra-abdominal pressure from CO2 insufflation pushes the diaphragm up, reduces lung compliance, and raises peak airway pressures, expect to need more pressure/PEEP than you did before insufflation

systemic vascular resistance typically rises with pneumoperitoneum, which can keep blood pressure looking normal or even elevated even as cardiac output and cerebral blood flow are actually falling, don't be falsely reassured by a normal BP alone
keeping end-tidal CO2 in a moderate range, roughly 30-35, has been shown to blunt some of the adverse cerebral perfusion pressure effects of combined pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg

internal jugular vein compression from prolonged head-down positioning raises intracranial pressure and has been linked to postoperative cognitive changes in some studies, watch the neck/face for progressive venous congestion over a long case
facial and airway edema from prolonged steep Trendelenburg is a real extubation-timing consideration, don't be surprised by it and have a plan (leak test, cautious extubation) for a long robotic case
sources: Kalmar AF, et al. Influence of steep Trendelenburg position and CO2 pneumoperitoneum on cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory homeostasis during robotic prostatectomy. Br J Anaesth. 2010.
Closhen D, et al. Effects of pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg position on intracranial pressure and cerebral blood flow. J Anaesthesiol Clin Pharmacol. 2023.

summary: CO2 pneumoperitoneum raises airway pressures and can raise systemic vascular resistance enough to mask a real fall in cardiac output and cerebral perfusion behind a normal-looking blood pressure — combined with steep Trendelenburg, it also raises intracranial pressure, which is why keeping end-tidal CO2 in a moderate range and watching for facial/airway edema over a long case both matter.
whyThisMatters: A normal or even elevated blood pressure during pneumoperitoneum can create false reassurance while cardiac output and cerebral blood flow are actually falling — because insufflation itself tends to raise systemic vascular resistance, blood pressure alone is a misleading proxy for adequate perfusion in this specific setting, which is exactly the kind of physiology that changes what a vigilant anesthesiologist watches during a long laparoscopic/robotic case.
clinicalTakeaway:
AIRWAY PRESSURES: expect higher peak airway pressures once pneumoperitoneum is established — the raised intra-abdominal pressure pushes the diaphragm cephalad and reduces lung/chest wall compliance. This is normal and expected, not itself a sign something is wrong, though it should be monitored and ventilator settings adjusted accordingly.

BLOOD PRESSURE: don't be falsely reassured by a normal or elevated blood pressure during pneumoperitoneum — systemic vascular resistance typically rises, which can mask a real fall in cardiac output and cerebral perfusion.

END-TIDAL CO2: target a moderate range (roughly 30-35 mmHg) during combined pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg, since this has been shown to help blunt some of the adverse cerebral perfusion pressure effects.

EDEMA: watch for progressive facial/airway edema and internal jugular venous congestion over a long steep-Trendelenburg case — both are real considerations for extubation timing and technique (a leak test, cautious extubation) and, in elderly patients particularly, have been linked to postoperative cognitive changes when jugular compression is significant.

items: Raised intra-abdominal pressure from CO2 insufflation pushes the diaphragm cephalad, reducing functional residual capacity and lung/chest wall compliance.

Expect HIGHER PEAK AIRWAY PRESSURES once pneumoperitoneum is established compared to before insufflation — this is an expected physiologic consequence, not inherently a sign of a problem, but it does mean ventilator settings (and alarm thresholds) may need adjustment to accommodate it.

Combined with steep Trendelenburg (which further shifts abdominal contents/diaphragm cephalad under gravity), the respiratory mechanics effect compounds — a case combining both (common in robotic pelvic surgery) often needs more active ventilator management than either factor alone.

body.text: Hemodynamic and cerebral effects — don't trust a normal blood pressure alone

Pneumoperitoneum typically RAISES systemic vascular resistance — this can keep blood pressure looking normal or even elevated even while cardiac output and cerebral blood flow are actually falling. A reassuring blood pressure number during insufflation does not necessarily mean perfusion is adequate.

items: The combination of pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg has been shown (via transcranial Doppler and related studies) to raise intracranial pressure and alter cerebral blood flow.

Maintaining end-tidal CO2 in a MODERATE range — roughly 30-35 mmHg — has been shown to help blunt some of the adverse cerebral perfusion pressure effects of this combined physiology; avoid both significant hypercapnia (which further raises ICP via cerebral vasodilation) and aggressive hyperventilation (which can excessively reduce cerebral blood flow) during these cases.

In elderly patients or those with longer case durations, watch specifically for internal jugular vein compression from prolonged head-down positioning — this has been associated in some studies with measurable postoperative cognitive changes, thought to relate to the combined effect of elevated intracranial pressure and impaired venous drainage.

body.text: Facial and airway edema — plan for extubation

Prolonged steep Trendelenburg positioning causes progressive facial, conjunctival, and airway soft-tissue edema from the sustained head-down gravitational fluid shift — this is a real and expected finding after a long robotic/laparoscopic case in this position, not a sign of a complication requiring investigation on its own.

It IS, however, a genuine extubation-timing consideration: have a plan for a cautious extubation approach (assessing for a cuff leak, being prepared for the possibility of upper airway swelling affecting the post-extubation airway) after a prolonged steep-Trendelenburg case, rather than treating extubation as routine regardless of case duration/position.
